text:
A: Hiya! Agnieszka, Wolverhampton.
B: Abena. Croydon.
A: Nice to meet you. I think you met Sana, from Bolton? She told me a lady told her off for not finishing her course. [laughs] Was you?
B: It was me. Somebody has to tell her. She's young. She keeps saying later, later.
A: No, I agree with you. She's lovely girl, but she needs somebody to push a bit.
B: Mm. You work in a school, she said?
A: Yeah, office, primary school. Twenty-five hours, term-time. Before that I was cleaning offices, two years, with degree in economics. So I told her also, plans don't always go when you want.
B: Cleaning with a degree. Yes. I know many like that. Nurses from Ghana doing cleaning. Here they don't care what you did at home.
A: Exactly. You came when?
B: 2003. For my husband. I gave up a lot to come. He gave up nothing to leave. That's it.
A: Oh. I'm sorry.
B: It's fine. Long time ago. You have a cross in your photo. You go to church?
A: Yeah, Polish Mass, most Sundays. Honestly more for the people than the rules, you know? After Mass everybody is talking, coffee, cake. Is like small Poland for one hour.
B: I go to a Ghanaian Methodist church. Same, it's for the people. But every week they want money. New roof, new van, a building fund. The big men on the committee drive nice cars. I ask, where is the roof?
A: [laughs] Every church is same, I think. Our priest also always has new project.
B: At least you can laugh. I sing in the choir, so I have to stay. Your family is in Poland?
A: My mum, seventy-eight, on her own in Łódź. And my sister. I think a lot, should I bring her here. But she don't speak English. She would be lonely in my house all day.
B: My mother is in Kumasi. My sister looks after her. And I am here washing other people's mothers. Sometimes I think about that too much.
A: Yeah. I understand. Is same feeling, you know? You look after everybody except your own.
B: Yes. Exactly that. I send money every month. It's not the same as being there.
A: No. But is something. My mum says, you have your life, is okay. I don't believe her. [laughs]
B: Mine says the same. They are lying to make us feel better.
A: [laughs] Probably. You go back?
B: Every two or three years. I'm building a house there, slowly, for when I retire. Block by block, when there's money.
A: That's a good plan. Better than mine. I don't have a plan, I just say we'll see.
B: We'll see is also a plan. Sometimes.
